253.title: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (1 of 7)
253.hook: twelve verses about one syllable, and the claim that it is all this
253.tomorrow: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (2 of 7)
253.howItsDone: Om is chanted by Hindus at the start and end of prayers, recitations and many rituals; the Mandukya Upanishad, with Gaudapada's verse commentary (Karika), is a central text in Advaita Vedanta study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ashvattha, and the end of the Katha: Nachiketa chose the good over the pleasant, and walked out of Death's house free.

Om. One syllable, hummed. It turns up at the start or end of a yoga class, on a meditation app, in a grandparent's room at dawn. Plenty of people say it without ever being told what it's supposed to mean. This week's Upanishad is entirely about that, in twelve verses. And its first line makes a claim so large it's worth reading twice.
screen: `OM, AT THE END OF CLASS.` → `ONE SYLLABLE, HUMMED.` → `WHAT DOES IT MEAN?`

segments.voice: The Mandukya opens: om. This syllable is all this. Then: here is its explanation. Everything that was, everything that is, everything that will be: all of it is om. And whatever is beyond the three times, that too is om. Notice: not om is a symbol of all this. Om is all this. You've met om before on this path, in camp one and in the Gita, where Krishna says that among words he is the one syllable. The Mandukya takes that seriously all the way down. Why a syllable? A sound comes out of silence, lives for a moment, and goes back into silence. A thought, a feeling, a whole day has that shape: it arises, stays a while, dissolves. Om is chanted as three sounds, a, u and m, flowing into each other, and then a silence after. This week, the Mandukya maps those three sounds onto the three states you live in every day, waking, dreaming and deep sleep. And the silence after them onto something it simply calls the fourth. That's the line for the week. Nobody is completely sure where the name comes from. Manduka means frog, and it may be the name of a Vedic teacher or school; tradition doesn't agree. Its weight in the tradition is plain, though. One later Upanishad, the Muktika, says that for the one seeking freedom, the Mandukya alone is enough. Twelve verses. One syllable. Everything.
screen: `OM: THIS SYLLABLE IS ALL THIS.` · `PAST, PRESENT, FUTURE, AND BEYOND.` · `A, U, M, AND THE SILENCE.` · `THE MANDUKYA ALONE IS ENOUGH.` · then, large: `OM.`

segments.voice: If you're comfortable, chant om once, slowly, out loud or under your breath: let it rise out of silence, hum for a while, fade, and then stay in the silence after it. If chanting isn't for you, listen to any sound in the room the same way: where it starts, how long it lasts, where it goes. Each time, rest in the quiet that follows.
The Mandukya Upanishad. Twelve verses on om, the syllable that is all this: past, present, future, and what's beyond time.
Your line: the fourth. It's the silence after the sound, and it's coming this week. Day two hundred fifty-three, done.

254.title: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (2 of 7)
254.hook: the self has four quarters, and the first is the waking world
254.tomorrow: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (3 of 7)
254.howItsDone: 'Ayam atma brahma' (Mandukya 2) is taught in Hindu Vedanta as one of four mahavakyas, great sayings, each drawn from a different Veda.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mandukya Upanishad began: om, this syllable is all this. Past, present, future, and beyond.

Every day you live in three different worlds, and you almost never think about it. In the morning you're here: coffee, emails, the bus. At night you're somewhere else entirely, flying, falling, late for an exam you never signed up for. And then, for a stretch, you're nowhere at all: deep, dreamless sleep, no world and no you, and you wake up saying, I slept well. The Mandukya takes those three worlds seriously. It starts with the one you're in right now.
screen: `THREE WORLDS A DAY.` → `HERE, THERE, NOWHERE.` → `THE ONE YOU'RE IN NOW.`

segments.voice: Verse two: all this is Brahman. This self, atman, is Brahman. And this self has four quarters. Catushpat: four feet, the way a cow has four feet, or a coin was split into four quarters. That middle sentence is bold. Ayam atma brahma: this self is Brahman. It's one of four famous great sayings in the Upanishads, the mahavakyas, and this is where it lives. The self you are and the ground of everything are the same, the Mandukya says, and then it maps that self in four parts. Verse three gives the first quarter: vaishvanara, the universal person, the one common to all people. Its field is the waking state. It knows outward: its attention faces the world. It has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, the text says; commentators explain the mouths as the senses, the organs of action, the breaths and the inner faculties, all the ways a person takes the world in. And it enjoys the gross: solid things you can touch and count. That's you, hearing this. The waking self. The Mandukya maps it to the first sound of om: a, the open mouth. Why start here? Because it's where you already are. The Mandukya doesn't say waking life is fake, or bad. It says it's one quarter. Real, full, and not the whole of you.
screen: `THIS SELF IS BRAHMAN.` · `FOUR QUARTERS.` · `THE FIRST: THE WAKING STATE.` · `KNOWING OUTWARD, ENJOYING THE GROSS.` · then, large: `ONE QUARTER, NOT THE WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Be fully in the waking state: your weight on the chair, the sounds around you, the air on your skin, the taste in your mouth. This is the first quarter, knowing outward; take it in with all nineteen mouths, as the text says. Then gently notice that you're aware of all of it, that the waking world is appearing to you, and rest there.
The Mandukya Upanishad. The self is Brahman, and it has four quarters. The first is vaishvanara: the waking state, knowing outward.
Your line: the fourth. Two more quarters to meet first, and then the fourth. See you tomorrow.

255.title: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (3 of 7)
255.hook: the second quarter: the dreaming self, the shining one
255.tomorrow: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (4 of 7)
255.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, the Mandukya and Gaudapada's Karika are studied together; the comparison between dreaming and waking is a classic subject of that study.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Mandukya Upanishad: this self is Brahman, with four quarters. The first is the waking state, knowing outward.

A childhood house, but with extra rooms. Someone who died, there at the table, and it all feels completely normal. Inside a dream, almost nothing gets questioned. The sky could be green and the teacher a dog, and the dreamer just nods. Then morning comes, and where did all of that come from? There was no house, no sky, no dog. A whole world came from somewhere inside. The Mandukya's second quarter is that dreamer.
screen: `THE HOUSE WITH EXTRA ROOMS.` → `NOBODY QUESTIONS IT.` → `A WHOLE WORLD, FROM INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Verse four: the second quarter is taijasa. Its field is the dream state. It knows inward. It too has seven limbs and nineteen mouths. And it enjoys the subtle. Taijasa means the shining one, from tejas, brilliance, radiance. Why shining? Commentators point to the dream itself: no sun, no lamp, and yet everything is seen. The dream world is lit from within, by the mind itself. Notice the flip from yesterday. The waking self knows outward and enjoys the gross, solid things. The dreaming self knows inward and enjoys the subtle: images, feelings, memories, made of mind-stuff. Same limbs and mouths, the same full set of experiences, but the whole world comes from inside. In the dream, it all felt completely real. Only on waking does the dreamer see where it came from. The Mandukya itself draws no conclusion from that. But a later teacher, Gaudapada, in his verse commentary on the Mandukya, asks: what if waking is a bit like that too? What if there's something that sees both states, the way you see the dream from the morning? That's where this week is headed. Whatever the answer, the verse makes one plain point: a person is not only a waking person. In the Mandukya's picture, every dreamer is a world-maker, lit from within. And in om, the second quarter is the second sound: u, the mouth rounding.
screen: `TAIJASA: THE SHINING ONE.` · `THE DREAM, LIT FROM WITHIN.` · `KNOWING INWARD, ENJOYING THE SUBTLE.` · `WHAT SEES BOTH STATES?` · then, large: `THE SECOND QUARTER.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let an image come, a place you love, a face, a color, and notice there's no outer light, yet you can see it: that's the shining one, lighting a world from inside. Let it fade and another come, and watch them the way you'd watch a dream, without getting pulled in. Then let them all go, and notice what was watching.
The Mandukya Upanishad. The second quarter is taijasa, the shining one: the dream state, knowing inward, lit from within.
Your line: the fourth. Every night, a whole world lit from within. Two hundred fifty-five days now.

256.title: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (4 of 7)
256.hook: the third quarter: deep sleep, where you want nothing and dream nothing
256.tomorrow: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (5 of 7)
256.howItsDone: Some Vedanta teachers use the everyday report 'I slept well' as a starting point for reflecting on deep sleep as the Mandukya's third quarter, prajna.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Mandukya Upanishad: the second quarter, taijasa, the shining one. The dream, lit from within.

People say it in the morning: I slept so well last night. But how would anyone know? In deep sleep there's no world, no dream, nothing to remember. And yet the report comes, with total confidence, as if it were the best part of the night. Something, it seems, was present enough to enjoy it. That deep, dreamless sleep is the Mandukya's third quarter. And the way it describes it is almost tender.
screen: `I SLEPT SO WELL.` → `HOW DO YOU KNOW?` → `THE THIRD QUARTER.`

segments.voice: Verse five: where the sleeper desires no desire and sees no dream, that is deep sleep, sushupta. The third quarter is prajna, the knowing one. Its field is deep sleep. It has become one; it's a single mass of knowing. It is made of bliss, anandamaya, and it enjoys bliss. Its mouth is consciousness. A mass of knowing, not a knower of things. In waking you know the world; in dream you know images. In deep sleep there are no objects at all, so the knowing isn't split up among them. It's gathered, like light with nothing to fall on. And made of bliss: commentators say that's why a person wakes up and says, I slept well. No wanting, no fear, no problems. Some commentators add: in deep sleep, the poor person and the king are exactly equal. Then verse six says something larger: this third quarter is the lord of all, the knower of all, the inner controller, the source of all; the beginning and the end of beings. Why? Shankara explains that the waking and dream worlds come out of it every morning and fold back into it every night. It's the seed they grow from. And the sound: m, the lips closing, the hum at the end of om, where the sound gathers before it stops. So now there are three: waking and a, dreaming and u, deep sleep and m. Tomorrow, what the Mandukya calls simply the fourth.
screen: `NO DESIRE, NO DREAM.` · `PRAJNA: A MASS OF KNOWING.` · `MADE OF BLISS.` · `THE SOURCE AND THE END.` · then, large: `THE THIRD QUARTER.`

segments.voice: Let the body get heavy, as if drifting toward sleep, but stay just awake, wanting nothing from these minutes, letting images and thoughts pass without following them. See if you can taste a little of what the text describes: no wanting, nothing to hold, just a quiet, gathered knowing. Don't try to fall asleep; just rest near it.
The Mandukya Upanishad. The third quarter is prajna: deep sleep, no desire, no dream, a single mass of knowing, made of bliss.
Your line: the fourth. Even dreamless sleep, the text says, is full of knowing. Day two hundred fifty-six, done.

257.title: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (5 of 7)
257.hook: the fourth: not a fourth state, but what the other three appear in
257.tomorrow: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (6 of 7)
257.howItsDone: Mandukya verse 7 is central to Advaita Vedanta, where 'the fourth' (turiya) names pure awareness; other Vedanta schools read the verse as describing the Lord beyond the three states.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Mandukya Upanishad: the third quarter, prajna, deep sleep. No desire, no dream, a mass of knowing, made of bliss.

Three films play on one movie screen, one after another: a busy city in daylight, then a dreamy, colorful fantasy, then a long black frame with nothing on it. Which of the three is the screen? None of them. The screen is what all three play on. It was there during the city, the fantasy and the black, and it never changed. The Mandukya has walked through waking, dreaming and deep sleep. Verse seven is the screen.
screen: `THREE FILMS ON ONE SCREEN.` → `WHICH ONE IS THE SCREEN?` → `NONE OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Verse seven describes the fourth quarter almost entirely by saying what it is not. Not knowing inward: that was the dream. Not knowing outward: that was waking. Not knowing both. Not a mass of knowing: that was deep sleep. Not knowing, and not unknowing. Then a string of more nots. Unseen. Beyond all dealings. Ungraspable. Without marks. Unthinkable. Unnameable. Its essence is the sure sense of the one self. In it the world comes to rest. Peaceful, shanta. Auspicious, shiva. Not two, advaita. This, they consider the fourth. That is the self. That is what is to be known. Two things to notice. First, the word. Later tradition calls it turiya, the fourth, but the verse itself just says caturtha, fourth, almost modestly. One way to read that: a grander name would make it one more thing. Second, the fourth isn't a fourth state you visit, like a trip after sleep. That's why the screen helps. Waking, dream and deep sleep come and go; the fourth is what they come and go in. On this reading, it's present right now, under this moment of waking, the way the screen is under the film. The word advaita, not two, names a whole school, Shankara's Advaita Vedanta, which reads this verse as its heart. Other schools read it differently, as describing the Lord's own nature beyond the three states.
screen: `NOT INWARD, NOT OUTWARD.` · `UNSEEN, UNTHINKABLE, UNNAMEABLE.` · `PEACEFUL, AUSPICIOUS, NOT TWO.` · `NOT A STATE: WHAT STATES APPEAR IN.` · then, large: `THE FOURTH.`

segments.voice: Notice that you're awake, then notice the awareness that knows you're awake; the Mandukya's map says the same awareness was there in last night's dreams, and in the deep sleep after them. Rest in that awareness itself, not in anything it's aware of. When a thought or sound arrives, let it play on the screen, and stay with the screen.
The Mandukya Upanishad. Its seventh verse: the fourth, peaceful, auspicious, not two. Not another state, but what all three appear in.
Your line: the fourth. The films keep changing, and the screen under them stays the same. Until tomorrow.

258.title: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (6 of 7)
258.hook: om, letter by letter: a, u, m
258.tomorrow: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (7 of 7)
258.howItsDone: Hindu teachers who follow the Mandukya instruct students to chant om as three sounds, a-u-m, followed by silence, following the Mandukya's mapping of the letters to waking, dream and deep sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the heart of the Mandukya Upanishad: the fourth. Peaceful, auspicious, not two; not a state, but what the states appear in.

Say om slowly, and pay attention to your mouth. It starts open, at the back of the throat: ah. Then the lips round forward: oo. Then they close: mmm. The sound travels from the back of the mouth to the front and shuts, as if it covers the whole instrument. The Mandukya does something else with it. Verses eight to eleven go back to where the Upanishad began, om, and take it apart, one letter at a time.
screen: `SAY IT SLOWLY.` → `AH, OO, MMM.` → `ONE LETTER AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Verse eight: this self, as a syllable, is om. The quarters are the letters, and the letters are the quarters: a, u and m. In Sanskrit, the o of om is made of a and u blended, so om is also written aum. Verse nine: waking, vaishvanara, is a, the first letter, because a is the first sound, and because it pervades: the text links it to words for obtaining and for being first. Whoever knows this, it says, obtains their desires and becomes first. Verse ten: dreaming, taijasa, is u, the second letter, linked to words for exaltation and for being in between. Dream sits between waking and deep sleep, the way u sits between a and m. Verse eleven: deep sleep, prajna, is m, the third letter, linked to words for measuring and for merging. In the commentators' picture, every night the waking and dreaming worlds are measured into deep sleep and merge there, the way a and u close into m. Some of these links are wordplay, a kind found across the Upanishads, where a sound suggests a meaning. They don't have to be etymology to fit neatly. So here's the whole map. Open mouth, waking. Rounding lips, dream. Closing lips, deep sleep. On this map, a single om walks through a whole day and night in one breath. And the fourth? It isn't a letter. There's nothing left in the mouth to make it. That's tomorrow.
screen: `THE LETTERS ARE THE QUARTERS.` · `A: WAKING, THE FIRST.` · `U: DREAM, IN BETWEEN.` · `M: DEEP SLEEP, MERGING.` · then, large: `A, U, M.`

segments.voice: If you're comfortable, chant om slowly three times, out loud or silently, feeling each sound in your mouth: on the ah, think waking; on the oo, dream; on the mmm, deep sleep. After the third, stay in the silence and add nothing. If chanting isn't your practice, simply breathe in three parts and rest after each out-breath.
The Mandukya Upanishad. Om, letter by letter: a is waking, u is dream, m is deep sleep. The fourth has no letter.
Your line: the fourth. A whole day and night, in one syllable. That's day two hundred fifty-eight.

259.title: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (7 of 7)
259.hook: the fourth has no letter: the silence after om, and four weeks of Upanishads
259.tomorrow: Karma yoga deep-dive: action as offering; Karma Yoga as taught by Vivekananda; work as worship (1 of 7)
259.howItsDone: Hindu practitioners who chant om are often taught to rest in the silence after the syllable, which the Mandukya's twelfth verse identifies with the fourth, the self beyond waking, dream and deep sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Mandukya Upanishad: om, letter by letter. A is waking, u is dream, m is deep sleep. And the fourth has no letter.

Musicians say the rests matter as much as the notes. A song with no silence in it is just noise. The pause before the last chorus, the beat of quiet after the final chord: that's where the music lands. The Mandukya has given three of its quarters a sound: a, u, m. The last verse is about the one that doesn't get one. And it closes this four-week stretch of the Upanishads with a rest.
screen: `THE RESTS MATTER.` → `THREE QUARTERS HAVE A SOUND.` → `THE LAST ONE DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: Verse twelve: the fourth is without a letter, amatra. Beyond all dealings. The world comes to rest in it. Auspicious. Not two. So om is the self. The one who knows this enters the self by the self. That's the end of the Upanishad. The fourth isn't a sound after m. It's the silence the whole syllable rises out of and falls back into. That's why teachers ask you to rest after chanting om: the silence isn't the end of the practice; it's the point. And that last line is lovely: you enter the self by the self. Not by going somewhere else. By being what you already are. The week, in one breath: om is all this, past, present, future and beyond. The self is Brahman, with four quarters. Waking, knowing outward. Dream, the shining one, lit from within. Deep sleep, a mass of knowing, made of bliss. The fourth: peaceful, auspicious, not two. The letters a, u, m, and the silence with no letter. And the four weeks. The Isha: all this is pervaded by the Lord; isha, nothing here is only mine. The Kena: by whom does the mind move? The one behind the ear, and the gods who learned their victory wasn't theirs. The Katha: a boy at Death's door choosing the good over the pleasant. The Mandukya: the fourth. Four short texts, every one pointing to the same place, behind the eye, underneath the three states, closer than breath. Next, three weeks on the three paths the Gita laid out: action, devotion and knowledge.

segments.voice: Breathe out slowly, all the way, and at the bottom of the out-breath, before the next one begins, rest in the small pause that nobody made. Let the in-breath come by itself, and each time the breath empties, meet the pause again, not stretching it, just noticing it; if a thought arrives, let it fade the way a sound does. If you'd like, chant om once at the start and let it fall into that same pause.
The Mandukya Upanishad. Twelve verses: om is all this; the self has four quarters; a, u, m for three of them, and silence for the fourth.
